subject: nineTailedKitsune
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: nine-tailed kitsune fox with spirit flames.
Style: high-fantasy anime.
reasoning:
I'm planning a nine-tailed kitsune fox module with spirit flames in a high-fantasy anime style, aiming for a substantial TypeScript file around 700-900 lines using the toon and glow kits, and need to be careful getting the SDK API calls correct since I can't test them directly.

I'm sketching the fox's proportions as a stylized quadruped, roughly 1.1m body length and 0.75m shoulder height, with nine fanning tails tipped in glowing blue-violet spirit flames, anime-style eyes, cream muzzle fur, a crescent moon forehead mark, and vermillion shrine markings. I'm setting up a coordinate system with the fox standing at y=0, no ground plane needed, and beginning to define the skeleton hierarchy starting from the hips and spine chain running to the chest and head.

Defining spine joints and loft stations...

Defining paths for the spine and neck chains...

I'm checking whether passing a ChainPoint directly as the `at` parameter works for parenting the head joint to neck.at(1) — confirming the spec example treats this as valid since ChainPoint carries the bone/point info needed.

Now I'm deciding the head joint's placement, parenting it to the last neck joint with coordinates that sit just past the neck's end and a forward-tilted direction. I'm also considering which direction words (right, left, up, down, forward, back) are valid for defining the head's local coordinate frame.

I'm settling on using named direction words consistently for joints and parts attached to the head, while treating `dir` values as model-space direction vectors like `[0,0,1]` for simplicity rather than frame-relative numbers, since I'm unsure of the exact semantics without testing.

Now I'm working out the quadruped leg placement for the fox — positioning hip/shoulder, knee/elbow, and foot/paw joints using chains or the `limb` IK helper, estimating segment lengths and target positions so the legs reach the floor at y=0 while keeping proportions roughly realistic for front and back legs.

I need to figure out how the limb function names its joints based on point count — with naming, if you give one more name than spans, the chain adds a tip joint. For a 3-span leg I'd get 3 joint names plus a tip, so I'm working out the naming scheme for front legs: shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw as the tip.

Now I'm figuring out where legs attach to the spine, mapping out the spine's joint points and positions so the front and hind legs parent to the right spine segments, and starting to think through the body loft stations along the spine.

For the loft I'm placing stations from rump to chest, each with explicit position, width, and height, lofted through the spine for skinning. Then for the nine tails, I'm planning a fan arrangement radiating backward from the rump using a ring helper around a backward-pointing axis, with each tail built as its own chain.

Thinking through the geometry more carefully, a ring at radius zero won't actually fan the tails apart since they'd all share the same base point, so I'm switching to manually computing nine spread-out yaw angles in the horizontal plane from a single root point near the rump, each defining a direction for that tail's chain to extend backward and outward.

Each tail becomes a four-point curved path with a slight upward sweep, with the outer tails fanning wide and the center ones staying closer to straight back, and I'm leaving a spot at the tip of each chain for a flame accent later.

I'm naming the tails as separate chains parented to the rump joint, sweeping them with a tapering radius so they're thick at the root and narrow toward the tip, colored in cream and orange with a flame shape glowing at each tip in cyan-violet tones.

For the flame geometry, I'll extrude two nested teardrop outlines at the tail tip—a pale cyan outer flame with glow and a brighter white inner flame—oriented so the flame's vertical axis follows the tail's tangent direction at that point.

The flame geometry should glow fine as a Part with flat-colored material. I'm also thinking about adding floating spirit wisps around the shoulders and above the head as small teardrop flames, plus a mystic gem crest on the forehead for the kitsune's fire motif.

For the head, I'm sketching a rounded skull scaled down with a tapering snout swept along a curved path from the skull front to the nose tip, using a radius function that narrows toward the tip and attaching everything to the head bone.

For fur paint I'm sketching a kitsune-themed toon palette: warm orange fur, cream for belly and muzzle, deep plum for socks and ear interiors, and a vermillion shrine-red for the gem accent, each defined with cel-shaded base and shadow tones.

Now I'm defining the spirit flame colors for a cyan-to-violet glow effect with layered core and outer shells at different glow strengths, and working out how to extrude the fox ear shape with a triangular outline, figuring out the orientation vectors so the ears tilt backward naturally on the skull.

I'm working out the local coordinate frame for placing the inner ear on the front face of the outer ear part, then opting for a simpler two-layer approach: an outer fur-colored ear and a slightly thicker inner outline for the cream-colored interior.

Actually, simpler approach: skip the extra geometry and just paint the inner-ear pattern directly using the outline coordinates, marking a narrow central region near the base as the inner color and the rest as fur. That avoids adding another extruded part entirely.

For eyes, I'll use a golden/amber iris to fit the kitsune theme, placing decals on the skull surface using azimuth and elevation around the head center to position them symmetrically on either side.

For the muzzle, I'm figuring out how to blend fur into a cream-colored lower face using a position-based edge paint, comparing the head's y-coordinate against a threshold to decide where fur gives way to cream.

I should wrap that edge paint inside a cel shader so the muzzle picks up the same lit/shadow treatment as the fur, letting the nested paint resolve correctly. Then I'm thinking about adding a small forehead marking, like a tiny vermillion gem stuck onto the head as a decorative accent.

For placement I'll use the skull surface's nearest-point lookup to find where the gem and any crescent mark should sit. I'm also considering a dark nose sphere at the snout tip, and whether to add fur-tuft cheek details or simplify and skip that for now.

I'm thinking through which 5-12 textures to actually generate: an eye texture, a shrine-style shimenawa rope with zigzag paper shide streamers around the neck for cultural flavor (built from an extruded zigzag outline), possibly fur-tuft cards for cheeks or tail tips, and layered flame-wisp cards with a radial flame texture to suggest spirit fire around the body.

I also want a paper talisman (ofuda) with a rune-like drawing hanging from the tail as another texture, while keeping total parts in the 180-340 range and the code around 600-800 lines to stay within budget. For the floating spirit flames, I'm planning small textured cards placed on frames around the head and back, oriented upward with glow applied for a ghostly fire effect.

Thinking through placement more, I'm considering putting the flame cards along the spine or rump as rising "hitodama" fire, adjusting lean and bend so they flare naturally, and applying a white/cyan tint so the flame texture's color reads through rather than defaulting to the nearest part's color.

For glow, I'll apply it directly to the returned card meshes array. For the nine tails, I'm setting up a paint function based on sweep coordinates so the tips shift to cream past a certain threshold while the rest stays in the base fur color, possibly adding a darker ring band near the tip for extra detail, keeping the logic simple rather than overcomplicating it with stripes.

Now I'm working out the geometry for how the tails fan out from a shared root point at the rump, computing angle and elevation per tail so the central ones rise higher and spread symmetrically, then building out each tail's path points using direction vectors scaled by length.

Writing tail chain and sweep code...

Working out the flame orientation...

Actually, extrudes might be overcomplicating this — cards could work better since they're double-sided and readable from multiple angles. Using `cross: true` gives crossed flame cards that read well from any viewing direction, which seems like the cheaper and more visually effective approach for the tail flames with a glow texture.

Settling on flow [1,0,0] with cross enabled for the flame cards, building frames at each tail tip using the tangent direction so flames grow along the tail. I'm checking that the cards call returns meshes compatible with the glow function so I can wrap the whole flame set in a glow effect.

For the flame texture itself, I'm sketching an SVG with a tapering flame silhouette filled by a vertical gradient going from violet-blue at the base through cyan to white near the tip, plus a brighter inner flame shape layered on top for depth, and a darker outline stroke sized to stay visible at the chosen raster resolution.

Now I'm planning a few small glowing orbs floating near the body as separate flame "parts" attached to the skeleton, then working out how to wrap a shimenawa rope talisman around the neck using a ring of points swept into a closed tube.

I'll place the ring at a chain point along the neck with a radius wide enough to clear the neck's thickness, and decide on colors — likely a pale straw/gold tone for the rope, using plain color strings for solid parts rather than cel shading since those don't need the anime-style treatment.

Now I'm working out the shide paper strips hanging off the rope — trying to construct a zigzag W-shaped outline for the hanging paper, which is proving fiddly to define as a clean non-crossing polygon, so I'm considering a simpler banded zigzag shape with a flat top edge and a jagged lower edge instead.

Still working out rope and shide placement logic...

I'm also debating whether to add a small hanging bell accessory on the rope, sketching out a lathe profile for its rounded shape and deciding where to position it relative to the neck rope.

For the overall look, I'm planning additional gold ornaments like a forehead gem and ear tufts, plus leg coloring that darkens toward the paws using a paint function based on height.

Building the leg chains with shoulder-elbow-wrist joints, sweeping them into tapered limbs, and attaching paw spheres scaled flatter so they sit naturally on the ground without clipping below the floor.

Checking the front leg target distance against segment lengths—0.71 needs lengths summing to about 0.73 to avoid overstretching the two-bone IK. For the front leg's three points (shoulder, elbow, paw), I need to make sure the joint names line up correctly with the two segments plus the foot tip.

For the hind leg with four points, I'll name them hip, knee, hock, and paw. I need a naming helper that appends L or R to each base joint name depending on which side of the body it's on, keeping all joint names unique across the skeleton.

For the neck, I'm building a short catmull-rom path from the chest point up through an intermediate point to the head, giving it two joints (neck1, neck2) parented off the spine's final joint so the chains connect properly. The neck gets a tapering radius for a furry ruff look, and I'm placing the head joint just past the neck's end point, offset toward the head's center.

I'm defining the skull as a sphere mesh attached to the head joint with slight asymmetric scaling for an anime-style rounded look, and considering whether to add cheek fluff using scattered fur-tuft cards on the skull surface.

For eyes, I'm planning to use the toon kit's animeEye helper with an orange iris and ink outline color, placing hits on the skull surface around a defined center point using azimuth and elevation offsets to position them symmetrically.

I'm computing the eye placement geometry, including mirroring for the left side, and checking that the eye decal size fits properly on the sphere surface, then moving on to think about ear placement.

For the ears, I'm working out the local coordinates using "left/up/forward" axis conventions, then figuring out how the ear plane should be oriented so it reads as a triangle when viewed from the front rather than appearing edge-on.

Working out ear outline shape and tapered thickness...

For the ear paint, I'm defining the inner surface as cream fur (fluffy inside) and outer as orange fur, based on the extrusion's local coordinates. Then I'm thinking through the head's fur paint, using a jagged furEdge boundary between cream cheek fur and orange fur, calibrated to the skull's joint position and radius so the cream patch sits in the lower third of the face.

For the snout, I'm setting cream fur on the underside and orange fur on top based on surface normal direction, then sketching the snout's catmull-rom path from the skull forward to a tapered tip to give it that classic fox muzzle protrusion.

I'm placing a small sphere at the snout's end for the nose, double-checking that the head joint's forward offset correctly nests the skull and neck geometry together. Now I'm thinking about adding cheek fur ruffs and a small forehead gem placed using the nearest surface point on the skin mesh.

I'm considering whether to add flame "wisps" rising from the head like a crown, but deciding against it since they'd clutter the ears -- better to leave the top of the head clear and add flame effects elsewhere instead.

Placing wisp flame cards and glowing orb spheres at the sides of the body to give a floating fire aura, then thinking through the tail sweeps and flame geometry plus a furred edge on the belly to accent the body coloring.

I'm now adding a paper ofuda talisman card tied near the chest with vermillion rune texture, attaching it to the neck bone position.

Figuring out exactly where to hang it on the rope — thinking of placing it at the bottom-facing rope item near the chin, alongside shide paper fan strips at neighboring rope positions so they don't overlap, with the ofuda plane oriented to hang downward facing forward.

Now I'm planning the ofuda texture itself: an SVG paper panel with cream background, red border, and vermillion runic characters rendered as central vertical text or simple glyph paths.

I'm counting textures so far — eye, flame, tuft, ofuda — and want to hit the 5-12 target, so I'm considering adding a forehead rune decal to replace the gem and maybe a second flame texture or a shide-paper zigzag pattern to round things out.

Settling on six distinct textures (eye, flame, wisp variant, tuft, ofuda, forehead seal decal) to give decent atlas variety, then moving on to actually writing the builder code — importing the right functions from the agentic-3js-builder SDK and setting up the scene structure.

Mapping out the toolkit's API surface: joints with parent/aim relationships, chains built from paths with configurable twist and segment counts, lofted and swept geometry for organic shapes, part/extrude/lathe for structural pieces, and cards/decals for applying the textures I'm planning.

I'm also defining the fox's color palette now, setting up cel-shaded materials for the fur, cream accents, dark socks, and other key coat colors.

Working through how the paint system nests—cel shading can wrap other paint results like furEdge patterns, so I'm tracing how layered fur edges and cream-colored sections resolve correctly through that recursive paint resolution.

I'm defining tail, leg, and sock paints with simple positional conditionals, being careful to underscore unused callback parameters to satisfy strict typechecking. Now I'm setting up the eye texture with amber iris colors and starting to build SVG textures for flame, wisp, and tuft elements.

Writing SVG gradient paths...

Making the crescent gold with a red gem and ink outline, then placing the seal decal on the forehead via a surface hit with inferred normal direction, sized small relative to the skull. For the shimenawa rope, I'm generating a ring of points around the neck, sweeping a closed Catmull-Rom path through them with rope coloring, then planning to attach shide paper strips at two side points and an ofuda talisman at the bottom to avoid overlap.

I'm positioning the shide strips using the rope item's frame location, orienting them with a downward outline, then considering adding a bell lathed near another rope point offset slightly below.

Actually, I decide to skip the bell entirely since it doesn't look right sitting at the top of the neck. For the ofuda, I'm placing a textured white plane along the neck bone, offset downward from one of the rope items, oriented to face forward — and I'm figuring out whether to attach it to the neck chain directly or specify a particular joint within it for more precise bone positioning.

Now I'm working out the nine tails procedurally — computing yaw and lift angles across the spread so they fan outward symmetrically, varying tail length and curvature based on distance from center, and building each tail's control points from a shared root position near the base of the neck, with slight upward and outward offsets at the tip for a natural flowing shape.

With roughly 50 joints total across tails, spine, neck, and legs, I'm well under the joint budget. I'm also placing small flame effects at each tail tip, orienting them using the tangent direction at the end of each tail's curve, and giving each tail a tapering radius so the root cluster looks dense and bushy while the tips thin out.

Now I'm scattering a handful of floating wisp cards and glowing orbs around the body at various offsets, giving them subtle bend and cross geometry so they look like drifting spirit flames, and adding glow to the orbs and flame cards so they read as bright light sources.

Moving on to legs, I'm writing a helper to name left/right limb bones, then looping over both sides to build front legs: creating limb joint paths, chaining them into named shoulder/elbow/paw bones as leg roles, sweeping a tapered tube along each for the leg geometry, and capping the paw with a flattened sphere "sock" shape.

Writing hind leg code...

Checking the front hip parenting against the spine joints, then setting up the spine chain itself as a child of hips using a catmull-rom path with three named joints. Now I'm lofting the torso body shape along the spine, defining width/height stations from rump to shoulder front, then working out how the neck path should connect from the chest's top-front point up to a head joint, adjusting the spine's end coordinates so the neck attaches smoothly.

I'm placing the head joint at the top of the neck with a forward/upward orientation, then computing the head's center position and skull radius to check proportions against the body — the result leans toward a big-headed, stylized kitsune look, which seems fine for this design. Now I'm positioning the ears relative to the head joint using lateral, upward, and forward offsets.

I'm checking that the ear base sits near the skull surface by comparing skull radius against the offset distances, adjusting the up/forward values so the ears sit naturally rather than floating or sinking too deep into the head geometry.

Now I'm working out the skull sphere's placement and scale relative to the head bone, deciding on reasonable segment counts for a small part like this, then sketching snout points by sweeping forward and down from the head center to shape the muzzle profile.

I'm recalculating these offsets relative to the head joint itself to keep skull, snout, and nose tip proportions consistent — making sure the snout tip extends a believable distance past the skull front and that the nose sphere sits right at its end, while checking eye placement doesn't collide with the snout base.

I'm also verifying vertical placement so eyes sit above the snout top, placing ears and the cream fur boundary for the muzzle/cheeks, and defining filters for forehead seal placement and cheek tuft scatter based on surface normals. Now I'm starting on the neck's sweep radius taper.

For the neck geometry, I'm shaping it to taper into the ruff and deciding how to layer the cream chest bib on top of the base fur paint, using surface normal checks (front-facing z) combined with height cutoffs so the chest and neck front read as cream while the rest stays furred. Working out tail fur tufts now: scattering small tuft cards along each tail sweep using frame points at a few parameters per tail, considering spikes or cones as fur tips instead of flat cards for a better silhouette.
